noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: practical: investigate photosynthesis, showing the evolution of oxygen from a water plant, the production of starch and the requirements of light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll

primer.text: You know photosynthesis needs light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll, and that glucose is stored as starch. This practical lesson proves each requirement with a classic test: bubbling pondweed for oxygen, foil-covered leaves for light, potassium hydroxide flasks for carbon dioxide, and iodine to reveal where starch was made.

lessons.title: Oxygen Evolution from Pondweed
lessons.opening: A water plant such as pondweed, submerged under an upturned funnel with a water-filled boiling tube above it, releases oxygen as it photosynthesises. The bubbles collect in the tube and displace the water, and a glowing splint relighting in the collected gas proves what it is; counting bubbles over time even measures the rate.
keyPoints: Oxygen gas is released by the photosynthesising pondweed.
Bubbles leave the cut stem and gather in the inverted boiling tube.
A glowing splint that relights identifies the collected gas as oxygen.
Bubble count or gas volume over time tracks the photosynthesis rate.
The apparatus comprises beaker, pondweed, funnel, boiling tube and splint.

low.restatement: Plant bubbles, tube collects, splint proves oxygen.
low.analogy: A diver's breathing apparatus in miniature — bubbles rise and are trapped.
low.examPointer: Name the splint test explicitly; it is the standard identification mark.

medium.restatement: The setup doubles as a rate meter: bubble frequency varies with light and carbon dioxide supply.
medium.analogy: Counting raindrops in a gauge to track the storm.
medium.examPointer: Use the rate angle when a question varies light intensity and asks for the effect.

check.stem: What proves the collected gas is oxygen?

options.text: A glowing splint relights when placed in the sample
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: The gas dissolves in the water
options.explanation: Oxygen collection is visible as bubbles.

options.text: The gas smells fresh
options.explanation: Smell identifies nothing here.

options.text: The water turns clear
options.explanation: No colour change occurs.

check.stem: Where do the oxygen bubbles originate?

options.text: From the cut end of the submerged pondweed stem
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: From the funnel's rim
options.explanation: The funnel only channels gas.

options.text: From the boiling tube's water
options.explanation: The tube collects, it does not generate.

options.text: From the beaker's surface
options.explanation: Surface air is not the source.

check.stem: How can the same setup measure the rate of photosynthesis?

options.text: By counting bubbles, or the collected volume, over a fixed time
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: By weighing the plant hourly
options.explanation: Mass change is not the read-out.

options.text: By timing the splint test
options.explanation: The splint test identifies gas, not rate.

options.text: By measuring water temperature
options.explanation: Temperature is not varied or measured here.

check.stem: Why must the plant be submerged under the funnel?

options.text: So released oxygen bubbles are channelled into the boiling tube for collection
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: To keep the plant from drying
options.explanation: Submersion is the natural state of pondweed.

options.text: To cool the plant
options.explanation: Cooling is not the funnel's function.

options.text: To add carbon dioxide to the water
options.explanation: The setup does not supply gas.

check.stem: Which apparatus item is reserved for the oxygen test itself?

options.text: The splint, lit and used to relight in the gas
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The cork borer
options.explanation: No cork borer appears in this setup.

options.text: The boiling tube holder
options.explanation: Holding hardware is not the test.

options.text: The ethanol
options.explanation: Ethanol belongs to the starch test.

check.stem: Name the test used to identify oxygen gas.
check.modelAnswer: The glowing splint test, which relights in the presence of oxygen.

check.stem: State what is collected in the inverted boiling tube.
check.modelAnswer: Oxygen gas released by the photosynthesising pondweed collects there, displacing water.

check.stem: Explain why bubble count rises when the lamp is moved closer.
check.modelAnswer: Because closer light raises the intensity reaching the plant, photosynthesis speeds up, and oxygen is released faster; the bubble stream thins out again only when another factor becomes limiting.

check.stem: A student's pondweed stops bubbling after an hour under bright light. Suggest the likely limiting factor.
check.modelAnswer: The most likely limiting factor is dissolved carbon dioxide, which the plant has exhausted from the water; light remains bright and temperature steady, so the scarcest resource — carbon dioxide — now caps the rate and the bubbling stops.

lessons.title: Testing a Leaf for Starch and Light
sourceHeadings: Method Part 2 - Testing the leaf for starch
lessons.opening: Glucose is made and quickly used, but starch persists where photosynthesis happened, so an iodine test for starch maps a leaf's photosynthesising zones. The leaf is boiled, bleached in hot ethanol, softened, and stained: blue-black where starch was stored, orange-brown where foil kept out the light.
keyPoints: Starch stored in chloroplasts marks where photosynthesis has occurred.
De-starching in a dark cupboard for a day clears existing starch.
Part of the leaf is covered with foil while the plant stands in sunlight.
Boiling water softens the leaf, hot ethanol removes the chlorophyll.
Iodine turns blue-black on starch and stays orange-brown without it.
The foil-covered area stays brown because it could not photosynthesise.

low.restatement: Cover, boil, bleach, stain: blue-black means starch, brown means none.
low.analogy: Developing a photograph — the treated areas reveal the pattern.
low.examPointer: List the five steps in order; the sequence carries marks.

medium.restatement: The ethanol step exists for observation, removing pigment so iodine colours read clearly, and the water bath handles ethanol's flammability safely.
medium.analogy: Washing a slide before staining it.
medium.examPointer: Justify the water bath — 'ethanol is highly flammable' earns the safety mark.

check.stem: Why is starch, not glucose, tested for in the leaf?

options.text: Glucose is used up or transported quickly, while starch persists where it was made
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Glucose is invisible to iodine only
options.explanation: The persistence of starch is the stated reason.

options.text: Glucose is toxic to the leaf
options.explanation: Glucose is the plant's own product.

options.text: Starch dissolves faster for testing
options.explanation: Starch is actually insoluble and stored.

check.stem: What is the purpose of de-starching the plant in a dark cupboard?

options.text: So any starch already present is used up and cannot confuse the result
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: To kill the leaf's cells
options.explanation: The leaf stays alive.

options.text: To make iodine react faster
options.explanation: De-starching affects the leaf, not the reagent.

options.text: To remove the chlorophyll early
options.explanation: Chlorophyll removal happens in ethanol later.

check.stem: Why is ethanol heated in a water bath rather than over a flame?

options.text: Ethanol catches fire easily, so it stays far from naked flames
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Water bath heats ethanol faster
options.explanation: Safety, not speed, is the reason.

options.text: Ethanol dissolves the boiling tube
options.explanation: Glass is unaffected.

options.text: Iodine decomposes over flames
options.explanation: Iodine is added later, at room temperature.

check.stem: What result does the foil-covered area of the leaf show after iodine?

options.text: It remains orange-brown, showing no starch was made there
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It turns blue-black like the rest
options.explanation: Only illuminated areas store starch.

options.text: It turns the leaf white
options.explanation: Bleaching happened earlier, for both areas.

options.text: It dissolves the leaf tissue
options.explanation: The leaf stays intact for staining.

check.stem: Why must chlorophyll be removed before staining?

options.text: So the iodine's colour change can be seen clearly against the pale leaf
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because chlorophyll destroys iodine
options.explanation: No such reaction is cited.

options.text: Because green leaves cannot absorb iodine
options.explanation: Absorption is fine; visibility is the issue.

options.text: Because ethanol needs a second use
options.explanation: The ethanol step is single-purpose.

check.stem: State the colour iodine shows in the presence of starch.
check.modelAnswer: Iodine turns the leaf blue-black where starch is present.

check.stem: Name the solvent used to remove chlorophyll from the leaf.
check.modelAnswer: Hot ethanol removes the green chlorophyll from the leaf.

check.stem: Explain why the foil experiment proves light is necessary for starch production.
check.modelAnswer: Because the same leaf, treated identically, stains blue-black only where light reached it and stays orange-brown under the foil; the single controlled difference is illumination, so light must be required for the photosynthesis that laid down the starch.

check.stem: A student forgets the de-starching step. Predict the result and the conclusion it threatens.
check.modelAnswer: Old starch from before the experiment may still stain blue-black even under the foil, making both areas blue-black; the student could wrongly conclude that light is unnecessary, when in fact residual starch blurred the test.

lessons.title: The Carbon Dioxide Experiment and CORMS
sourceHeadings: Applying CORMS evaluation to practical work
lessons.opening: One leaf in a flask of potassium hydroxide, one control leaf in an empty flask, both de-starched and left in bright light: the treated leaf lacks carbon dioxide because the chemical absorbs it from the air. Iodine then shows starch only on the control leaf, proving carbon dioxide is required for photosynthesis.
keyPoints: Potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide from the air inside the flask.
A second leaf in a flask without the chemical serves as the control.
Both leaves are de-starched before the plant stands in bright light.
The treated leaf stays orange-brown after iodine; the control turns blue-black.
Both leaves come from the same de-starched plant, so only carbon dioxide differs.

low.restatement: No carbon dioxide, no starch: the chemical flask proves it.
low.analogy: Silencing one singer to show the choir needs every voice.
low.examPointer: Always name the control flask and its purpose in the answer.

medium.restatement: The design isolates one variable — carbon dioxide — while light, temperature and the leaf itself are matched.
medium.analogy: A twin study: same everything, one difference.
medium.examPointer: Identify the control and explain why it must exist.

check.stem: What does potassium hydroxide do inside the conical flask?

options.text: It absorbs carbon dioxide from the surrounding air
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: It releases carbon dioxide
options.explanation: It removes the gas, which is the point.

options.text: It supplies water to the leaf
options.explanation: The leaf is attached to the plant, not the flask liquid.

options.text: It stains the leaf for starch
options.explanation: Staining is iodine's job later.

check.stem: Why is a flask without potassium hydroxide included?

options.text: As a control, to show the leaf photosynthesises when carbon dioxide is available
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: To double the starch yield
options.explanation: Yield is not the design's purpose.

options.text: To keep the plant moist
options.explanation: Moisture comes from the plant itself.

options.text: To absorb oxygen instead
options.explanation: The chemical's role is carbon dioxide removal in the treated flask only.

check.stem: What result does the potassium hydroxide leaf give after iodine?

options.text: It remains orange-brown, showing no starch was produced
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It turns blue-black like the control
options.explanation: Without carbon dioxide no starch was made.

options.text: It turns the solution green
options.explanation: The leaf does not colour the flask.

options.text: It shows the five-step colour change
options.explanation: That diagram belongs to the starch-test method.

check.stem: Which steps prepare each leaf before the light exposure?

options.text: De-starching the whole plant for a day in darkness
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Boiling the leaves immediately
options.explanation: Boiling happens only at the starch-test stage.

options.text: Covering one leaf with foil
options.explanation: Foil belongs to the light experiment.

options.text: Adding iodine before the light
options.explanation: Iodine is the final test, after the exposure.

check.stem: What conclusion does the paired-flask experiment support?

options.text: Carbon dioxide is necessary for photosynthesis and starch production
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Light is unnecessary when flasks are used
options.explanation: Light was provided to both leaves.

options.text: Potassium hydroxide is a plant nutrient
options.explanation: It is an absorbent chemical, not a nutrient.

options.text: Starch can be made without photosynthesis
options.explanation: The treated leaf's failure shows the opposite.

check.stem: State the role of the control flask in this experiment.
check.modelAnswer: The control flask holds no potassium hydroxide, so its leaf photosynthesises normally for comparison.

check.stem: Name the chemical that absorbs carbon dioxide in this setup.
check.modelAnswer: Potassium hydroxide solution absorbs the carbon dioxide inside the flask.

check.stem: Explain why both leaves must come from the same de-starched plant.
check.modelAnswer: Because starting starch levels and plant condition must match; a leaf from another plant, or one still holding starch, would confound the iodine result and break the one-variable design that makes the conclusion trustworthy.

check.stem: The treated leaf surprisingly stains blue-black. Evaluate the investigation.
check.modelAnswer: A blue-black treated leaf suggests the carbon dioxide absorption failed — perhaps the flask leaked or the potassium hydroxide was exhausted — so the investigation should be repeated with a sealed flask and fresh chemical before any conclusion is drawn.

glossary.definition: Leaving a plant in darkness so its leaves use up stored starch before an experiment.
Relighting a splint inside a gas sample to prove the gas is oxygen.
The chemical that absorbs carbon dioxide from the air inside the experimental flask.
